title: Skyscrapers: 'Scuse me while I kiss the sky
summary: Josh and Chuck explore skyscrapers: the ancient quest for height, the rise of skyscrapers in the late 1800s (Home Life building in Chicago often cited as first), how iron and steel (Bessemer and open hearth processes) enabled taller buildings, steel skeleton construction, spread footings and grillage foundations, elevators (Otis, 1857 New York department store), fire sprinklers, window placement in offices, wind sway and tuned mass dampers, the City Corp (Citicorp) building fix, design trends from Art Deco to International Style, Willis (Sears) Tower, Miami's One Thousand Museum, criticisms of glass towers and short building lifespans, wood skyscrapers like Brock Commons, and the race for the world's tallest buildings (Burj Khalifa, Jeddah Tower, Dubai Tower). The episode closes with listener mail about Occam's razor.

entities.name: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat

segments.title: Opening banter and tour dates
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce fall tour dates in Salt Lake City, Phoenix and Melbourne, apologize for using the word prostitute, and introduce the skyscraper topic.

segments.name: content
segments.title: Quest for height and origins of skyscrapers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the long history of building tall, from ancient structures to the late 1800s, the Home Life building in Chicago, and how the word skyscraper came to mean anything tall.

segments.title: Iron, steel and the limits of brick and mortar
segments.summary: Brick and mortar limited building height. Iron and steel, including the Bessemer and open hearth processes, allowed lighter, stronger, thinner materials and taller buildings with smaller footprints.

segments.title: Steel skeleton and foundations
segments.summary: Skyscrapers use a steel skeleton of riveted columns and girders that carries the building's weight down to foundations. Each column sits on a spread footing of cast iron plate, grillage and concrete, anchored to clay or bedrock.

segments.title: Functionality, stairs and elevators
segments.summary: Skyscrapers must function for workers and businesses, which makes elevators essential. Elevator shafts take up floor space, so builders balance elevator count against floors and occupants. Otis elevators appeared in New York in 1857.

segments.title: Fire sprinklers, office comfort and atriums
segments.summary: Fire sprinklers became mandatory in commercial high-rises after deadly hotel fires. Designers aimed to keep occupants near windows, and the hosts discuss indoor atriums and gardens.

segments.title: Wind sway and tuned mass dampers
segments.summary: Skyscrapers sway in wind. The City Corp Center needed an emergency fix. Engineers design for occupant comfort, and tuned mass dampers, including concrete discs, water vats and magnetorheological fluid, counter the sway.

segments.title: Architectural design trends and criticisms
segments.summary: Skyscraper styles moved from Art Deco to International Style and modern designs. Examples include the Willis Tower, One World Trade Center, and One Thousand Museum Tower in Miami. Critics question glass towers and short building lifespans, and wooden skyscrapers like Brock Commons are discussed.

segments.title: World's tallest buildings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the race for the tallest building, including the Burj Khalifa, the Jeddah Tower and a Dubai tower, plus the lack of an official definition of skyscraper categories.

segments.title: Listener mail: Occam's razor
segments.summary: A listener named Camilla clarifies that Occam's razor favors the most parsimonious explanation, meaning fewest assumptions, rather than simply the simplest.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact information and sign off.
